items.stem: Why are alloys like nichrome used in heating devices like electric iron, toasters, etc.?
items.answer: Because the resistivity of alloys is higher than that of the pure metals which form the alloys. Resistivity changes less rapidly with changes in temperature. Also, alloys do not oxidise readily at high temperature.

items.stem: Which has higher resistance, a 50 W lamp bulb or a 25 W lamp bulb, and how many times?

items.stem: Let the resistance of an electrical device remain constant, while the potential difference across its two ends decreases to one fourth of its initial value. What change will occur in the current through it? State the law which helps us in solving the above stated question.
items.answer: According to Ohm's law, V = IR. Since the resistance is constant and the potential difference is decreased to one-fourth of its initial value, the current through the device also decreases to one-fourth of its initial value. Ohm's law states that at constant temperature the potential difference (V) across a conductor in an electric circuit is directly proportional to the electric current (I) flowing through it.

items.stem: Why are the heating elements of electric toasters and electric irons made of an alloy rather than a pure metal?
items.answer: The resistivity of an alloy is generally higher than that of its constituent metals, so an alloy produces much more heat for the same current. Alloys also do not oxidise (burn) readily at higher temperatures. Therefore the conductors of electric heating devices such as toasters and electric irons are made of an alloy rather than a pure metal.

items.answer: The electrical resistivity of a material is the resistance offered to the flow of current by a conductor of that material of unit length and unit area of cross-section. items.stem: Distinguish between the terms overloading and short-circuiting as used in domestic circuits.
items.answer: (i) Short-circuiting occurs when a live wire comes in contact with a neutral wire, whereas overloading occurs when many electrical appliances of high power ratings are operated at the same time. (ii) In short-circuiting a very large current flows through the circuit because the resistance of the path formed where the two wires touch is very small; in overloading a large current is drawn from the electric supply because of the simultaneous use of many appliances.

items.stem: A piece of wire of resistance 20 Ω is drawn out so that its length is increased to twice its original length. Calculate the resistance of the wire in the new situation.
items.answer: Let the original length be l, so R₀ = ρl/A = 20 Ω. The new length l' = 2l and, as the volume of the wire stays constant, Al = A'l' gives A' = A/2. The new resistance Rₙ = ρl'/A' = ρ(2l)/(A/2) = 4(ρl/A) = 4R₀ = 4 × 20 = 80 Ω.

items.stem: A copper wire has a diameter of 0.5 mm and a resistivity of 1.6 × 10⁻⁶ ohm-cm. How much of this wire would be necessary to make a resistance of 10 ohm?
items.answer: Radius of the wire r = d/2 = 0.5/2 = 0.25 mm = 0.025 cm. Since R = ρl/A, the length l = RA/ρ = Rπr²/ρ = 10 × (22/7) × (0.025)²/(1.6 × 10⁻⁶) = 122.67 cm.

items.stem: A copper wire of length 3 m and area of cross-section 1.7 × 10⁻⁶ m² has a resistance of 3 × 10⁻² ohms. Calculate the resistivity of copper.
items.answer: Given l = 3 m, A = 1.7 × 10⁻⁶ m² and R = 3 × 10⁻² Ω. From R = ρl/A, ρ = RA/l = (3 × 10⁻² × 1.7 × 10⁻⁶)/3 = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m.

items.stem: (a) What is meant by electric resistance of a conductor? (b) A wire of length L and resistance R is stretched so that the length is doubled and the area of cross section is halved. How will (i) resistance change and (ii) resistivity change?
items.answer: (a) The resistance of a conductor means the obstruction it offers to the flow of current through it. (b) The new length L' = 2L and the new area A' = A/2. (i) R' = ρL'/A' = ρ(2L)/(A/2) = 4ρL/A = 4R, so the resistance becomes four times. (ii) Resistivity depends only on the material of the wire, so the resistivity remains the same.

items.stem: How do currents in different resistors vary if they are connected in parallel?
items.answer: In a parallel combination the same potential difference acts across every resistor, so the currents in the different resistors are inversely proportional to their resistances: the higher the resistance of a branch, the less is the current through it. The total current is the sum of the currents flowing in the different branches.

items.stem: If five resistances each of value 0.5 ohm are connected in series, what will be the resultant resistance?
items.answer: Resultant resistance R = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ + R₄ + R₅ = (0.5 + 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.5) Ω = 2.5 Ω.

items.stem: Suppose a 6 volt battery is connected across a lamp whose resistance is 20 ohm through a variable resistor as shown in the given figure. If the current in the circuit is 0.25 A, find out the resistance of the variable resistor.
items.answer: Let R₁ be the resistance required from the variable resistor, so the total resistance in the circuit R = 20 Ω + R₁. By Ohm's law I = V/R, so 0.25 A = 6 V/(20 Ω + R₁), giving 20 + R₁ = 6/0.25 = 24 and R₁ = 4 ohm.

items.stem: How are three resistors joined in parallel? What is the potential difference across each resistor joined in parallel?

items.stem: (a) What is the total resistance of n resistors each of resistance R connected in (i) series, (ii) parallel? (b) Calculate the resultant resistance of 3 resistors 3 Ω, 4 Ω and 12 Ω connected in parallel.

items.stem: Write the applications of the heating effect of current.
items.answer: (a) The heating effect of current is utilised in many electrical appliances such as the room heater, electric iron, electric toaster and electric lamp. (b) It is also used in the electric fuse, which melts and breaks the circuit when too large a current flows.

items.stem: How much work is done during the flow of current for a given time in a wire?
items.answer: Since a conductor offers resistance to the flow of current, work has to be done continuously to move the electrons and maintain the current. The work done in carrying a charge Q through a potential difference V is W = Q × V. As Q = I × t, W = V × I × t, and by Ohm's law V = IR, so W = I²Rt. Since energy is the capacity to do work, the electrical energy converted is H = I²Rt.

items.stem: Express Joule's law of heating mathematically. What is the resistance of a 12 m wire having radius 2 × 10⁻⁴ m and specific resistivity 3.14 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m?
items.answer: In accordance with Joule's law of heating, if a current I flows through a resistor of resistance R for a time t, the heat produced across the resistor is H = I²Rt joules. For the given wire, R = ρl/A = ρl/(πr²) = (12 × 3.14 × 10⁻⁸)/(3.14 × 4 × 10⁻⁸) = 3 Ω.

items.answer: The rate at which electrical energy is consumed, or converted into heat, is known as electric power. P = W/t = I²Rt/t = I²R, and also P = I × V, i.e. power = current × potential difference. Its SI unit is the watt.

items.stem: (i) What is meant by resistance of a conductor? Define its SI unit. (ii) List two factors on which the resistance of a rectangular conductor depends. (iii) How will the resistance of a wire be affected if (1) its length is doubled, and (2) its radius is also doubled? Give justification for your answer.
items.answer: (i) Resistance is the property of a conductor by which it resists the flow of charge through it. Numerically it is the ratio of the potential difference across the conductor to the current flowing through it. Its SI unit is the ohm (Ω): a conductor has a resistance of 1 ohm if a current of 1 ampere flows through it when the potential difference across it is 1 volt. (ii) The resistance depends on (1) the length of the conductor and (2) the area of cross-section of the conductor. (iii) (1) Resistance is directly proportional to length, so if the length is doubled the resistance is also doubled. (2) Resistance is inversely proportional to the area of cross-section; if the radius is doubled the area becomes four times larger, so the resistance becomes one-fourth.

(a) List the factors on which the resistance of a conductor in the shape of a wire depends.
(b) Why are metals good conductors of electricity whereas glass is a bad conductor of electricity? Give reason.
(c) Why are alloys commonly used in electrical heating devices? Give reason.
items.answer:
(a) The resistance of a conductor depends directly on its length, is inversely proportional to its area of cross-section, is directly proportional to the temperature, and depends on the nature (material) of the conductor.
(b) Metals have free electrons which can move and conduct electricity, whereas glass does not have free electrons which can flow freely to conduct electricity.
(c) The resistivity of an alloy is generally higher than that of a pure metal, and alloys do not oxidise (burn) readily at higher temperatures. Therefore the conductors of electric heating devices, such as toasters and electric irons, are made of an alloy rather than a pure metal.

items.stem: State the factors on which the resistance of a cylindrical conductor depends. How will the resistance of a conductor change if it is stretched so that its length is doubled?
items.answer: The resistance of a cylindrical conductor is directly proportional to its length l and inversely proportional to its area of cross-section A, i.e. R ∝ l and R ∝ 1/A. Combining, R ∝ l/A, so R = ρl/A, where ρ is the resistivity of the material. On stretching, the volume of the wire stays constant, so Al = A′(2l), giving A′ = A/2. The new resistance R′ = ρ(2l)/(A/2) = 4ρl/A = 4R, i.e. 4 times the original resistance.

items.stem: State Joule's law of heating. List two special characteristics of a heating element wire. An electric iron consumes energy at the rate of 880 W when the heating is at the maximum rate and 440 W when the heating is at the minimum rate. The applied voltage is 220 V. Calculate the current and resistance in each case.
items.answer: Joule's law: if a current I flows through a resistor of resistance R for a time t, the heat produced in the resistor is H = I²Rt joules. Two characteristics of a heating element wire: (i) it must not melt at high temperature (high melting point), and (ii) it has high resistivity. For the electric iron, V = 220 V. items.stem: Derive an expression for the equivalent resistance when two resistors of resistance R₁ and R₂ are connected in parallel.
items.answer: Consider two resistances R₁ and R₂ connected in parallel across a potential difference V. When the current I reaches the junction a, it splits into I₁ through R₁ and I₂ through R₂. Since charge is conserved, the current entering a equals the current leaving it: I = I₁ + I₂ ...(1). As the resistors are in parallel, the potential difference across each is the same, so by Ohm's law I₁ = V/R₁ and I₂ = V/R₂. Substituting in (1), I = V/R₁ + V/R₂ ...(2). If R_p is the equivalent resistance of the combination, then I = V/R_p ...(3). From (2) and (3), V/R_p = V/R₁ + V/R₂, hence 1/R_p = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂.

items.stem:
In an electric circuit three bulbs of 100 W each are connected in series to a source. In another circuit a set of three bulbs of the same wattage are connected in parallel to the same source.
(i) Will the bulbs in the two circuits glow with the same brightness? Justify your answer.
(ii) Now, let one bulb in both the circuits get fused. Will the rest of the bulbs continue to glow in each circuit? Give reason for your answer.
items.answer:
(i) Let the resistance of each bulb be R and the source voltage be V.
Case (1) Series combination:
R_equ = R + R + R = 3R
Current in each bulb, I = V/3R
Case (2) Parallel combination:
Net current, I_equ = 3V/R
The current divides equally among the three bulbs, so the current in each bulb is
I = I_equ/3 = 3V/(R × 3) = V/R
As power P = V²/R, P is inversely proportional to R. Hence the bulbs in case (2) will glow with greater brightness, because the power is 3 times more than that in case (1).
(ii) In case (1), if one bulb gets fused the rest of the bulbs will not glow, because in a series circuit the voltage across the circuit is the sum of the voltages across each bulb and the circuit is broken. But in case (2), the parallel combination, the voltage across each bulb is the same, so all the other bulbs will glow — the interruption in the fused bulb does not affect the voltage across the others.

(a) Derive the relation for the equivalent resistance when three resistors of resistances R₁, R₂ and R₃ are connected in parallel.
(b) Find the minimum resistance that can be made using four resistors, each of 20 Ω.
items.answer:
(a) In a parallel combination the total current I is equal to the sum of the separate currents:
I = I₁ + I₂ + I₃ …(1)
Let R_p be the equivalent resistance of the parallel combination of resistors. Applying Ohm's law,
I = V/R_p, and I₁ = V/R₁, I₂ = V/R₂, I₃ = V/R₃
Substituting in equation (1),
V/R_p = V/R₁ + V/R₂ + V/R₃
1/R_p = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃
Hence, if n resistors are connected in parallel the equivalent resistance is
1/R_eq = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃ + … + 1/Rₙ
(b) To get the minimum resistance all the resistors must be connected in parallel. Hence
1/R = 1/20 + 1/20 + 1/20 + 1/20 = 4/20
R = 20/4 = 5 ohm

(a) What is meant by the statement, “The resistance of a conductor is one ohm”?
(b) Define electric power. Write an expression relating electric power, potential difference and resistance.

items.answer:
(a) Ohm's law states that the current flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference maintained across the two ends of the conductor at constant temperature and pressure. If I is the current and V the potential difference, then V ∝ I, so V = IR, where R is the proportionality constant called resistance.
As per the question the resistance of the conductor is 1 ohm. Let V = 1 volt and I = 1 A, then R = 1 ohm. Hence the resistance is said to be 1 ohm if 1 ampere of current flows through a circuit due to a potential difference of 1 volt.
(b) Electric power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transformed in an electrical circuit. P = VI, where P is the power, V the potential difference and I the electric current. Using Ohm's law it can also be written as P = I²R and P = V²/R, where R is the resistance in the circuit.
(c) Let x be the number of 132 Ω resistors. Supply voltage V = 220 volt, current I = 5 A. If R is the equivalent resistance of the combination,

From Ohm's law: 132/x = 220/5 = 44
132 = 44x, so x = 132/44 = 3
So the answer is 3 resistors.

items.stem:
(i) Consider a conductor of resistance R, length L, thickness d and resistivity ρ. Now this conductor is cut into four equal parts. What will be the new resistivity of each of these parts? Why?
(ii) Find the resistance if all of these parts are connected in: (a) Parallel (b) Series
(iii) Out of the combinations of resistors mentioned above in the previous part, for a given voltage which combination will consume more power and why?
items.answer:
(i) The resistivity will not change, as it depends only on the nature of the material of the conductor and on the temperature. It does not depend on the length of the conductor.
(ii) Let the length of the conductor AB = L. When the conductor is cut into four equal parts, the length of each part = L/4.
Since R = ρL/A, the resistance of each part is
R′ = ρL/(4A) = (1/4)(ρL/A) = R/4
(a) When all four parts are connected in parallel:
1/R_p = 1/R′ + 1/R′ + 1/R′ + 1/R′ = 4/R + 4/R + 4/R + 4/R = 16/R
R_p = R/16
(b) When all four parts are connected in series:
R_S = R/4 + R/4 + R/4 + R/4 = 4R/4 = R
(iii) Since P = V²/R_eqv, if R_eqv is less the power consumed will be more. In the given case R_eqv is smaller for the parallel combination, so the parallel combination will consume more power.

(b) Two lamps, one rated 100 W; 220 V and the other 60 W; 220 V, are connected in parallel to the electric mains supply. Find the current drawn by the two bulbs from the line, if the supply voltage is 220 V.

(a) According to Joule's law of heating, the heat produced in a wire is directly proportional to (i) the square of the current, I², (ii) the resistance of the wire, R, and (iii) the time t for which the current is passed. Thus the heat produced in the wire by a current I in time t is

Second lamp: I₂ = P₂/V = 60/220 = 0.27 A
So, total current = I₁ + I₂ = 0.45 + 0.27 = 0.72 A

items.stem:
(a) Define electric current. Write down the formula which relates electric current, electric charge and time.
(b) An electric bulb draws a current of 0.75 A for 15 minutes. Calculate the amount of electric charge that flows through the circuit.
items.answer:
(a) The electric current is a flow of electric charges, called electrons, in a conductor such as a metal wire. The magnitude of the electric current in a conductor is the amount of electric charge passing through a given point of the conductor in one second. If a charge of Q coulombs flows through a conductor in time t seconds, then the magnitude I of the electric current flowing through it is given by
I = Q/t
(b) Given, current I = 0.75 A and time t = 15 min = 15 × 60 s = 900 s.
Now, I = Q/t
0.75 = Q/900
Q = 0.75 × 900
Therefore the charge, Q = 675 coulombs.

items.stem: Define electric power. Write and define the S.I. unit of electric power. Derive the formula for electric power.
items.answer:
The electric work done per unit time is called electric power.
Electric power = Electric work done / Time taken, i.e. P = W/t
Electric power is also defined as the electric energy consumed per unit time: P = E/t
The S.I. unit of electric power is the watt. When one joule of energy is used for one second, the electric power is equal to one watt.
Derivation of electric power: we know that the electric work done is
W = V × I × t
So, P = VIt/t
P = VI
That is, electric power in watts = volts × ampere.
Also, since V = IR,
P = IR × I = I²R
and since I = V/R,
P = V²/R

items.stem: Describe an experiment to study the factors on which the resistance of a conducting wire depends. What is the effect of temperature on the resistance of a given conductor? For a given material, which of the two wires, thick or thin (having the same length), has less resistance? Why?
items.answer:
(a) Connect a circuit consisting of a cell, an ammeter, a wire of a material of high resistance — for example nichrome of length L (marked 1 in the figure) — and a key. Insert the key and note the current in the ammeter. Replace the wire by another one having the same thickness but of length 2L (marked 2). We note that the current has now decreased to one half, showing that the current depends on the length of the wire. Now take a thicker nichrome wire, i.e. of larger cross-sectional area but of the same length L (marked 3); we find that the current in the ammeter has increased, indicating that the flow of current depends on the cross-sectional area of the wire. Finally, instead of nichrome, take a wire of another material having the same length and the same cross-sectional area (marked 4); we find that the current in the ammeter has changed. This shows that the flow of current from the same source also depends on the material of the wire.
(b) The resistance of all pure metals increases on raising the temperature and decreases on lowering the temperature, provided the length, cross-sectional area and material of the conductor remain the same.
(c) The thicker wire will have less resistance than the thinner wire, because resistance is inversely proportional to the area of cross-section of the wire.

items.stem: Two resistances when connected in series give a resultant value of 9 Ω. The same resistances when connected in parallel give a resultant value of 2 Ω. Calculate the value of each resistance.
items.answer:
Let R₁ and R₂ be the two resistances.
In series: R₁ + R₂ = 9 …(1)
In parallel: 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ = 1/2, i.e. (R₁ + R₂)/(R₁R₂) = 1/2
From equation (1), 9/(R₁R₂) = 1/2, so R₁R₂ = 18
Now (R₁ − R₂)² = (R₁ + R₂)² − 4R₁R₂ = (9)² − 4 × 18 = 81 − 72 = 9
Thus R₁ − R₂ = 3 …(2)
Adding equations (1) and (2):
2R₁ = 12, so R₁ = 6 Ω
Substituting in equation (1): 6 + R₂ = 9, so R₂ = 9 − 6 = 3 Ω
Hence the two resistances are 6 Ω and 3 Ω.

(a) Resistors are given as R₁ = 10 Ω, R₂ = 20 Ω and R₃ = 30 Ω. Calculate the effective resistance when they are connected in series. Also calculate the current flowing when the combination is connected to a 6 V battery.
(b) Three resistors R₁, R₂ and R₃ are connected in series to a battery. Draw the circuit diagram showing the arrangement. Derive an expression for the equivalent resistance of the combination.
items.answer:
(a) In a series combination the effective resistance is
R = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ = 10 + 20 + 30 = 60 Ω
When this combination is connected to a 6 V battery, the current is
I = V/R = 6/60 = 1/10 A = 0.1 A
(b) Let the potential differences across the resistors R₁, R₂ and R₃ be V₁, V₂ and V₃ respectively, and let I be the current through the circuit. In a series circuit the current through each resistor is the same, I, and the potential difference V across the combination is equal to the sum of the potential differences across the individual resistors:
V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃ …(1)
If the resistors are replaced by an equivalent single resistor R such that the potential difference across it is V and the current I remains the same, then applying Ohm's law to the whole circuit and to the three resistors separately,
V = IR and V₁ = IR₁, V₂ = IR₂, V₃ = IR₃
Substituting in equation (1),
IR = IR₁ + IR₂ + IR₃
R = R₁ + R₂ + R₃

items.stem:
(a) How many 330 Ω resistances in parallel are required to carry 20 A on a 220 V line?
(b) Name a component used to regulate current without changing the voltage source.
(c) A 10 Ω resistance wire is doubled on it. Calculate the new resistance of the wire.
items.answer:
(a) As we know, R = V/I = 220/20 = 11 Ω.
Let n resistors of 330 Ω be required. For n equal resistors in parallel,
1/R_p = n/R, i.e. R_p = R/n
11 = 330/n
n = 330/11 = 30
So 30 resistors of 330 Ω are required.
(b) A variable resistance, or rheostat.
(c) Originally, R = ρ l/A = 10 Ω.
After doubling the wire on itself its length becomes l′ = l/2 and its area A′ = 2A. So
R′ = ρ l′/A′ = ρ (l/2)/(2A) = (1/4) ρ l/A = (1/4) R = (1/4) × 10 = 2.5 Ω

items.stem:
(a) State Ohm's law. Express it mathematically.
(b) Write symbols used in electric circuits to represent: (i) variable resistance (ii) voltmeter.
(c) An electric bulb is rated 220 V and 100 W. When it is operated on 110 V, what will be the power consumed?
items.answer:
(a) Ohm's law states that the current flowing in a conductor is directly proportional to the voltage applied across the ends of the conductor, keeping the temperature constant.
According to Ohm's law, V ∝ I; mathematically V = IR,
where V = voltage applied, in volts; I = current flowing in the circuit, in amperes; R = resistance of the conductor (the proportionality constant).
(b) (i) A variable resistance (rheostat) is drawn as a resistor with an arrow through it. (ii) A voltmeter is drawn as a circle enclosing the letter V.
(c) Resistance of the bulb,
R = V²/P = (220 V × 220 V)/(100 W) = 484 Ω
The power consumed by the bulb when it is operated on 110 V is
P = V²/R = (110 × 110)/484 = 25 W

Part (b)'s symbols survive only as figures inside the solution, so they are described in words; those figures are solution-side and are not attached.

items.stem:
A piece of wire having resistance R is cut into four equal parts.
(a) How will the resistance of each part compare with the original resistance?
(b) If the four parts are placed in parallel, how will the joint resistance compare with the resistance of the original wire?
items.answer:
(a) We know that R ∝ l. So, when the wire is cut into four equal parts, the resistance of each part is 1/4th of the original resistance. Hence
R₁ = R/4, R₂ = R/4, R₃ = R/4 and R₄ = R/4
(b) When these four parts are joined in parallel,
1/R′ = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃ + 1/R₄ = 4/R + 4/R + 4/R + 4/R = 16/R
R′ = R/16
The joint resistance is now 1/16th part of the original resistance.

items.stem: A current of 1 ampere flows in a series circuit containing an electric lamp and a conductor of 5 Ω when connected to a 10 V battery. Calculate the resistance of the electric lamp. Now, if a resistance of 10 Ω is connected in parallel with this series combination, what change (if any) in the current flowing through the 5 Ω conductor and the potential difference across the lamp will take place? Give reason. Draw the circuit diagram.
items.answer:
In the series circuit, I = 1 A, R₁ = 5 Ω and V = 10 volt. Let the lamp's resistance be R₂.
V = IR = I(R₁ + R₂)
R₂ = V/I − R₁ = 10 − 5 = 5 Ω
So the resistance of the electric lamp is 5 Ω.
If a resistance of 10 Ω is now connected in parallel with the above series combination, the equivalent resistance of the circuit is
1/R = 1/10 + 1/R_s, where R_s = 5 + 5 = 10 Ω
1/R = 1/10 + 1/10
R = 5 Ω
The series branch is still connected directly across the same 10 V supply, so the current through it is still 10/10 = 1 A. Hence there will be no change of current through the 5 Ω conductor.
Also, the potential difference across the lamp equals the same share of the circuit's potential difference as before (the supply being 10 V), so there will be no change in the potential difference across the lamp.

Its closing lines ('Also, potential difference across the lamp = Potential difference of the circuit = 10 V') print over the page break on p58. In the parallel step the book reuses the symbol R₁ for the newly added 10 Ω resistor. items.stem:
Find out the following in the electric circuit given in the figure:
(a) Effective resistance of the two 8 Ω resistors in the combination.
(b) Current flowing through the 4 Ω resistor.
(c) Potential difference across the 4 Ω resistance.
(d) Power dissipated in the 4 Ω resistor.
(e) Difference in ammeter readings, if any.
items.answer:
(a) The effective resistance of the two resistances in parallel combination is given by
1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ = (R₁ + R₂)/(R₁R₂)
R = R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂) = (8 × 8)/(8 + 8) = 4 Ω
(b) Current flowing through the 4 Ω resistor (as printed),
I = V/R = 8/4 = 2 A
(c) Potential difference across the 4 Ω resistor (as printed),
V = IR = 2 × 4 = 8 V
(d) Power dissipated in the 4 Ω resistor (as printed),
P = I²R = 2² × 4 = 16 W
(e) No difference can be seen in the ammeters' readings, as the same current flows through each element in a series circuit.
items.ocr: Parts (b)-(d) of the printed solution contradict the circuit and the book's own part (a). The figure was inspected: the 4 Ω resistor is in series with the 8 Ω and 8 Ω parallel pair (effective 4 Ω, part (a)) across the 8 V battery, so the circuit resistance is 4 + 4 = 8 Ω and the current is 8/8 = 1 A, which puts 4 V across the 4 Ω resistor and dissipates 4 W in it. The book divides the full 8 V by 4 Ω alone and prints 2 A, 8 V and 16 W — that would drop the whole supply across the 4 Ω resistor and leave nothing across the parallel pair. The printed values are reproduced and flagged rather than silently corrected. Part (e) stands: the loop is a series circuit, so both ammeters read the same.

items.stem:
(a) Derive an expression for the equivalent resistance of three resistors R₁, R₂ and R₃ connected in parallel.
(b) Fuses of 3 A, 5 A and 10 A are available. Calculate and select the fuse for operating an electric iron of 1 kW power at a 220 V line.
items.answer:
(a) In a parallel arrangement the total current I is equal to the sum of the separate currents through each branch of the combination:
I = I₁ + I₂ + I₃
I = V/R₁ + V/R₂ + V/R₃
I/V = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃
Let R_p be the equivalent resistance of the parallel combination, so that R_p = V/I. Then
1/R_p = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃
(b) Given P = 1 kW = 1000 W and V = 220 V.
I = P/V = 1000/220 = 4.5 A
So the suitable fuse is the 5 A fuse.

The printed list of fuses reads 'Fuse of 3 A, 5 , 5 A and 10 A'; the stray '5 ,' is a duplicated fragment and was dropped, leaving 3 A, 5 A and 10 A. Read the following case based passage and answer the questions given after the passage.

A room has two tube lights, a fan and a TV. Each tube light draws 40 W, the fan draws 80 W and the TV draws 60 W on the average. The tube lights are kept on for five hours, the fan for twelve hours and the TV for eight hours every day. The rate for electrical energy is ₹ 3.10 per kWh.

(i) Calculate the energy consumed by each tube light in a day.
(ii) What is the total energy consumed in a day?
(iii) Find the cost of electricity used in this room in a 30-day month.
(iv) What quantities determine the rate at which energy is delivered by current?
items.answer:
(i) For each tube light, Power P = 40 W = 40/1000 kW.
Energy consumed by each tube light in a day = P × t = (40/1000 kW) × 5 h = 0.2 kWh.

(ii) Energy consumed by the tube lights in a day = 2 × 0.2 kWh = 0.4 kWh.
Energy consumed by the fan in a day = (80/1000) kW × 12 h = 0.96 kWh.
Energy consumed by the TV in a day = (60/1000) kW × 8 h = 0.48 kWh.
Total energy consumed in a day = 0.4 + 0.96 + 0.48 = 1.84 kWh.

(iii) Energy consumed in 30 days = 1.84 × 30 = 55.2 kWh.
Cost of electricity = ₹ 3.10 × 55.2 = ₹ 171.12.

(iv) The rate at which energy is delivered is determined by (a) the potential difference across the conductor and (b) the current flowing in the circuit.
items.ocr: Currency glyph printed as a LaTeX \yen / \mathfrak{F} artefact; restored to ₹. The LaTeX array carrying the (ii) total collapsed to '0.2 × 0.2 kWh + 0.96 kWh + 0.48 kWh' with the sum dropped; the printed (iii) line ('= 1 84 kWh' and '₹ 3.1 × 55.2 = ₹ 171.12') confirms the total is 1.84 kWh and the 30-day figure 55.2 kWh, so the arithmetic was restored from the book's own numbers.

items.stem:
Read the following case based passage and answer the questions given after the passage.

In the series combination, the resistances are joined end to end. For a series combination of resistors, Rₛ = ΣRᵢ and the current through each resistor is the same but the potential differences between their ends are different according to their resistance. When two or more resistors are combined in such a way that their first ends are connected to one point and the second ends to another point, they form a parallel combination. In a parallel combination of resistors, 1/Rₚ = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + … and the potential drop across each resistor is the same but the currents in the different resistances are different.

(i) If we connect n bulbs each with a rated power P in series, what is the total power consumed by the combination at rated current?
(ii) If we connect n bulbs each with a rated power P in parallel, what is the total power consumed by the combination at rated voltage?
(iii) The power consumed by n equal resistances in parallel is x times that of the power consumed in series, if the voltage supply is the same. Find the value of x.
(iv) If resistors 4 Ω, 5 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in series with a 5 V battery, calculate the total power consumed by the combination.
items.answer:
(i) When resistors are in series combination, Rₛ = R₁ + R₂ + … + Rₙ, so
V²/Pₛ = V₁²/P₁ + V₂²/P₂ + … + Vₙ²/Pₙ.
When the bulbs are of equal power, V²/Pₛ = nV²/P, hence Pₛ = P/n.

(ii) When resistors are in parallel combination, 1/Rₚ = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + … + 1/Rₙ, so
Pₚ/V² = P₁/V² + P₂/V² + … + Pₙ/V², i.e. Pₚ = P₁ + P₂ + … + Pₙ = nP.

(iii) Power consumed in series, Pₛ = V²/(nR), and in parallel, Pₚ = V²/(R/n) = nV²/R.
Since Pₚ = xPₛ, V²/(R/n) = x · V²/(nR), giving x = n².

(iv) Power consumed, P = V²/Rₑq = V²/(R₁ + R₂ + R₃) = (5)²/(4 + 5 + 6) = 25/15 = 5/3 W ≈ 1.67 W.
items.ocr: MinerU printed the parallel power as 'Pp = ^R/nh' and stopped the (iii) derivation at 'V²/(R/n) = x V²/(nR)' without stating x; the value x = n² follows directly from the book's own last line. LaTeX fractions and subscripts rewritten to Unicode.

Read the following case based passage and answer the questions given after the passage.

In household electric circuits, the mains supply is delivered to our homes using a three core cable. The cable consists of three wires — live wire, neutral wire and earth wire. The live wire is at a potential difference of 220 V for the domestic supply and the potential difference between the live and the neutral wire is 220 volts. The live wire is connected to the electric meter through a fuse or a circuit breaker of higher rating. The neutral wire is connected directly to the electric meter.

(i) What is a short circuit?
(ii) How are switches connected in the circuit?
(iii) What is the usual current rating of the fuse wire in the line if electric iron, geysers, room heater etc. are in use?
(iv) Why is earthing of all electrical appliances recommended?
items.answer:
(i) The condition when the live wire comes in direct contact with the neutral wire, so that a high current flows, is called a short circuit.

(ii) Switches are connected in the live wire, because when the switch is in the off position no point of the connected electrical appliance will be at the higher potential (220 V).

(iii) A fuse of rating 15 A is usually used for appliances such as electric iron, geysers and room heaters etc.

(iv) The earthing of any electrical appliance is done to protect the user from any accidental electrical shock due to leakage of current.

Read the following case based passage and answer the questions given after the passage.

A D.C. generator, also called a D.C. dynamo, converts mechanical energy into electrical energy (D.C.). It works on the principle that when a coil rotates in a uniform magnetic field, a current is induced in the coil. The direction of the induced current is determined by Fleming's right hand rule. The schematic diagram of a D.C. generator is as shown in the figure.

(i) The essential difference between an A.C. generator and a D.C. generator is that
(a) A.C. generator has an electromagnet while a D.C. generator has a permanent magnet.
(b) D.C. generator will generate a higher voltage.
(c) A.C. generator will generate a higher voltage.
(d) A.C. generator has slip rings while the D.C. generator has a commutator.
(ii) What is the frequency of D.C.?
(iii) What type of dynamo is used in a bicycle?
(iv) A D.C. motor is rotating in the clockwise direction. How can the direction of rotation be reversed?
items.answer:
(i) (d) A.C. generator has slip rings while the D.C. generator has a commutator.

(ii) Zero.

(iii) We use a D.C. dynamo in a bicycle.

(iv) The direction of rotation of the motor can be reversed by reversing the direction of the current through the coil. This can be achieved by interchanging the terminals of the battery connected to the brushes of the motor.

Read the following case based passage and answer the questions given after the passage.

Resistance of a conductor depends on the length, area of cross-section and nature of the material of the conductor. When a conductor is stretched (increased in its length), then its area of cross-section decreases accordingly but the volume (i.e. area × length) of the conductor remains the same. Resistivity of a conductor, ρ = RA/l, where A = area of cross-section of the conductor and l = length of the conductor.

(i) What do you mean by resistivity?
(ii) The SI unit of resistivity is
(a) ohm (Ω)
(b) ohm-metre (Ω-metre)
(c) ohm²-metre (Ω²-m)
(d) ohm-metre (Ω-m)
(iii) Write one difference between resistance and resistivity.
(iv) The resistance (R) of a wire whose length is halved and area of cross-section (A) is doubled, its new resistance (R′) will be
(a) R
(b) R/2
(c) R/4
(d) R/8
items.answer:
(i) Resistivity is defined as the resistance of a conductor of unit length and unit area of cross-section.

(ii) (b) The SI unit of resistivity is ohm-metre.

(iii) Resistance is that property of a conductor by virtue of which it opposes or resists the flow of charges through it; its SI unit is Ω. Resistivity is the characteristic property of the material of the conductor and varies only if its temperature changes; its SI unit is Ω-metre.

(iv) (c) R/4.
Initially, R = ρl/A (ρ = resistivity).
New length l′ = l/2 and new area of cross-section A′ = 2A (given).
New resistance R′ = ρ (l/2)/(2A) = ρl/4A = R/4.

items.stem:
Read the following case based passage and answer the questions given after the passage.

An electrician is a tradesman specialising in electrical wiring of buildings, transmission lines, stationary machines and related equipment. An electrician may be employed in the installation of new electrical components or the maintenance and repair of existing electrical infrastructure. An electrician has made the electric circuit of a house in such a way that if a fan is closed, the lamps also stop glowing.

(i) What is the defect in this type of circuit wiring? Why?
(ii) Two resistances R₁ and R₂ are connected turn by turn in parallel and in series. In which case will the resultant resistance be less than either of the individual resistances?
(iii) Which is the better way to connect lights and other appliances in a domestic circuit — series connection or parallel connection?
(iv) In which type of combination will different resistors have an equal value of electric current through them?
items.answer:
(i) The electrician has made a series connection of all the lamps in the electric circuit of the house, because of which, if one lamp gets fused, all the other lamps would stop working. This is due to the fact that when devices are connected in series, then if one device fails, the circuit gets broken and all the devices in that circuit stop working.

(ii) In parallel, because the resultant resistance in a parallel circuit is R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂), whereas in series the equivalent resistance is R₁ + R₂. Hence the equivalent resistance is less in a parallel circuit.

(iii) Parallel connection is a better way to connect lights and other appliances in a domestic circuit. It is because when we connect a number of devices in parallel combination, each device gets the same potential and hence keeps on working even if other devices stop working.

(iv) In series combination, different resistors will have an equal value of electric current.

Read the following case based passage and answer the questions given after the passage.

Current only flows through a component of a circuit if a potential difference (voltage) is put across it. The bigger the potential difference across its ends, the bigger the current flow. This is because there is a steeper 'electric slope' in place to make the charge slide down — steeper slope, faster slide. The equation below is used to work out the resistance of a component from measurements of the current flowing through it and the potential difference across its ends:

V = IR

where V = potential difference in volts (V), I = current in amps (A) and R = resistance in ohms (Ω).

There are four factors that affect the resistance of a wire: length, area, material and temperature. Resistance is proportional to length. If you take wires of different lengths and give each a particular potential difference across its ends, the longer the wire the fewer volts each centimetre of it will get. This means that the 'electric slope' that makes the electrons move gets less steep as the wire gets longer, so current decreases with increased length and resistance increases. Resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area. The bigger the cross-sectional area of the wire, the greater the number of electrons that experience the 'electric slope' from the potential difference. Resistance depends on the material the wire is made of — the more tightly an atom holds on to its outermost electrons the harder it will be to make a current flow. Resistance increases with the temperature of the wire; the hotter wire has a larger resistance because of increased vibration of the atomic lattice: R = R₀(1 + αT), where α is the temperature coefficient of resistance.

Answer the following questions.

(i) How does the resistance of metals change with increase in temperature?
(ii) There are two conductors X and Y of the same material, having lengths L and 2L and having radii r and r/2 respectively. What will be the ratio of their resistances?
(iii) Two wires of equal lengths, one of copper and the other of manganin, have the same resistance. Which wire will be thicker?
(iv) Draw the V–I graph for a metal piece at a given temperature.
items.answer:
(i) Resistance increases with the increase in temperature.

(ii) Resistance of conductor X, R_X = ρL/(πr²).
Resistance of conductor Y, R_Y = ρ(2L)/(π(r/2)²) = 8ρL/(πr²).
Therefore R_Y = 8R_X, i.e. R_X : R_Y = 1 : 8.

(iii) The manganin wire will be thicker than the copper wire.

(iv) The V–I graph for a metal piece at a given temperature is a straight line passing through the origin (V directly proportional to I).

There are some important points regarding parallel and series combinations of resistances. When two or more resistors are connected in series, the total resistance of the combination is equal to the sum of all the individual resistances. When two or more resistors are connected in series, the same current flows through each resistor. When a number of resistors are connected in series, the voltage across the combination (i.e. the voltage of the battery in the circuit) is equal to the sum of the voltage drops (or potential differences) across each individual resistor.

R = 10/3 Ω
